chapters.title: The main line: 3...e6 and the Nb5 jump
chapters.intro: After 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 e6 4.e3, Black's most natural moves all meet the same idea: Nb5. The knight and the f4 bishop both hit c7, so Black has to spend time defending it, and if Black plays ...Bd6 the knight can take the bishop. Black's best answers are to trade on f4, to check on b4, to prevent Nb5 with ...a6, or to cover c7 with ...Na6. Learn which version of Nb5 fits each one, and when to switch plans to h4 or the e4 break instead. Note that 3...e6 4.e3 c5 is the same position as 3...c5 4.e3 e6, covered in the next chapter.

chapters.title: 3...g6 and 3...Nc6
chapters.intro: Against the fianchetto with 3...g6, the Jobava has a direct plan: h4 and h5, and if Black castles early the h-file opens and Bh6 takes off his best defender. Against 3...Nc6, Nb5 is stronger than ever, because the c6 knight no longer guards c7. Black must answer with the ...e5 pawn sacrifice, and every quiet move loses to Nxc7.

chapters.intro: Most 1...Nf6 players will transpose with 2...d5. Against the others: 2...g6 gets the Qd2, O-O-O and Bh6 attack; 2...e6 is met by 3.Bf4, keeping the system; and 2...c5 is answered with 3.d5, taking space.

courses.name: Jobava London
courses.tagline: The London with its gloves off. Nc3, Bf4, Nb5, and castle long.
courses.description: The Jobava London, or Rapport-Jobava System, is the London's aggressive cousin. Instead of the quiet c3 and Nbd2, White plays Nc3 and Bf4 and aims straight at Black's weak points. The knight jumps to b5 to hit c7 with the f4 bishop, the queen goes to d2 or d3, White often castles queenside and throws the h-pawn up the board, and the e4 break or f3 with g4 punishes an early ...Bf5. This course teaches the main 3...e6 lines with Nb5 and Black's answers ...Bd6, ...Bb4, ...a6 and ...Na6, the sharp 3...c5 with ...Qb6 and ...Qa5, the ...Bf5 and ...c6 setups, the King's Indian style ...g6, the tricky 3...Nc6, and every 1...Nf6 move order. Along the way you learn the traps that make this system so dangerous at club level: Nc7 forks, h-file sacrifices, and the one move order mistake you must never make.

chapters.title: The main setup vs ...d5
chapters.intro: Against 1...d5 and ...e6 you build the London pyramid: pawns on c3, d4 and e3, bishop on f4, knights on f3 and d2, bishop on d3. When Black offers to trade bishops with ...Bd6, drop back to g3. Then you have two plans. The attacking plan is Ne5, f4, Qf3 and a kingside pawn storm with g4. The central plan is the e4 break, which works best when Black's pieces are passive. This chapter also shows the three traps that catch Black most often in the main line: ...Nd7 and ...b6 at the wrong moment, and ...Ne4 when d5 is not protected.

chapters.title: Against 1...Nf6, the Indians and the Dutch

Against the Dutch with 1...f5, the e4 square is Black's outpost, so your plans change: against the Stonewall trade dark-squared bishops and take e5 for yourself, and against the Leningrad play c4 and fight on the queenside.

chapters.title: Deeper theory: Black's best tries against the setup
chapters.intro: Strong players don't just copy the main line. They hunt your bishop with ...Nh5, trade it with ...Ne4, develop their light bishop before ...e6 and then hit b2, or open the c-file with ...cxd4. The setup stays the same; what changes is knowing the one or two precise moves each idea asks for. Two themes recur. Against ...Nh5, Bg5 gets out with tempo on the queen. And once Black's light-squared bishop leaves c8, b7 is loose, and Qb3 hits it.

chapters.title: Offbeat replies
chapters.intro: Some players avoid main lines altogether: the Chigorin-style 2...Nc6, the Old Indian with ...d6 and ...Nbd7, the Modern with 1...g6, the Englund Gambit with 1...e5, and flank moves like 1...b6, 1...b5 and 1...c5. Each has a simple answer you can learn once. Against the flank moves, step out of the London and take the whole centre with e4.

courses.name: London System
courses.tagline: One setup against everything. Bf4, e3, c3, Nf3, Nbd2, Bd3, and go.
courses.description: The London is the easiest repertoire in chess to learn: you put your pieces on the same squares in almost every game. But a setup is only half a repertoire, so this course also teaches what to do once the pieces are out: the Ne5 and f4 attack with Qf3 and g4, the e4 break, and queenside play with b3 or b4. You learn the exact moves against Black's sharpest tries: ...c5 with ...Qb6, the ...c4 clamp, early ...Bf5 and ...Bg4, the ...Nh5 bishop hunt in all its forms, ...Ne4, ...cxd4 structures, Queen's Indian, King's Indian, Grünfeld and Old Indian setups, the Dutch in its Classical, Stonewall and Leningrad forms, and offbeat first moves like the Englund Gambit, 1...b6, 1...b5 and the Benoni. Along the way Kittu shows you the traps Black falls into most often.

chapters.title: Queen's Gambit Declined: 2...e6
chapters.intro: Black supports d5 with ...e6 and builds a rock-solid position. You develop with Nc3, pin the f6 knight with Bg5, and play e3 and Nf3. Black's problem piece is the c8 bishop, shut in behind the e6 pawn, and Black's whole game is about freeing it with ...b6, ...dxc4 and ...e5, or ...c5. Your long-term plans depend on the pawn structure. If d5 is exchanged and Black has pawns on c6 and d5, you get the Carlsbad structure, where the minority attack with b4 and b5 creates a weak black pawn on the queenside. If Black ends up with an isolated d-pawn or hanging pawns on c5 and d5, you blockade them and attack them with pieces.

chapters.title: The Tarrasch: the isolated queen's pawn
chapters.intro: With 3...c5 Black accepts an isolated d-pawn in return for free and active piece play. This chapter teaches you the other side of IQP positions. A pawn on d5 that no other pawn can defend is a long-term weakness. Blockade it on d4 with a knight, put your bishop on g2 to aim at it, and trade pieces, because every exchange takes away Black's activity and leaves the weak pawn behind. If Black's pawns end up on c6 and d5 instead, they are hanging pawns, and the c5 square and the c-file become yours.

chapters.intro: Black defends d5 with ...c6, keeping the c8 bishop free to come out to f5 or g4. You develop with Nf3 and Nc3. If Black takes on c4 you play a4 to stop ...b5, then win the pawn back with e3 and Bxc4 and build a big centre with e4. If Black plays ...e6 first, it's the Semi-Slav, a very solid structure where you play calmly with e3 and Qc2 and prepare e4. If Black develops the bishop early, Qb3 hitting b7 is often the punishment.

Keep pieces on the board, aim at Black's king, and look for the d5 break.

chapters.title: Offbeat defences and traps
chapters.intro: The Albin, Chigorin, Baltic, Marshall and Symmetrical try to catch you unprepared. Each one gives up something positional for activity, so learn one sensible setup against each and you'll be better. Watch out for the Lasker Trap in the Albin: never play an early e3 there.

courses.name: Queen's Gambit
courses.tagline: The classical way to play 1.d4: pressure d5 and squeeze.
courses.description: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 offers a pawn to pull Black's centre apart. This course covers every serious reply, and above all it teaches the pawn structures that decide these games: the Carlsbad structure and the minority attack, the isolated queen's pawn, and hanging pawns. You'll learn the Queen's Gambit Declined (Orthodox, Tartakower, Lasker, Capablanca, Cambridge Springs, the Exchange structure and the Manhattan), the Tarrasch, the Slav, Semi-Slav and Noteboom, the Queen's Gambit Accepted, and the Albin, Chigorin, Baltic, Marshall and Symmetrical Defences. Along the way you'll learn the Elephant Trap and the Lasker Trap so you never fall for them.

chapters.title: Advance Variation: 3.e5
chapters.intro: White grabs space with e5 and builds a pawn chain from b2 to e5. Unlike in the French, you develop the bishop to f5 before playing ...e6, so your structure has no bad bishop. Then you attack the base of the chain with ...c5, bring a knight to c6 and the queen to b6, and pile up on d4. Against the quiet Short system you develop calmly; against the aggressive lines with g4 or h4, you keep the bishop safe on g6 or h7 and counter in the centre with ...c5, because a flank attack is best met by central action.

chapters.title: Classical: 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5
chapters.intro: White plays 3.Nc3 (or 3.Nd2). You take on e4 and develop the bishop with tempo on the knight. In the main line, White chases the bishop with Ng3 and h4; you meet h4 with ...h6, let the bishop retreat to h7, and trade it on d3. Then you build the famous fortress: pawns on c6, e6, f7, g7, knights on d7 and f6, and castle on whichever side is safer. Your freeing break is ...c5, or ...e5 when White's knights are slow. chapters.title: Exchange and Panov: 3.exd5
chapters.intro: After 3.exd5 cxd5 the pawns are symmetrical or White goes for an isolated pawn. In the Panov (c4) White gets an isolated d-pawn: it gives White activity and the e5 square, but it is a long-term weakness. You blockade on d5, trade pieces, and aim for an endgame where the pawn falls.

chapters.title: Two Knights and the Fantasy
chapters.intro: White can avoid the main lines with 2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3 (the Two Knights) or 3.f3 (the Fantasy). Against the Two Knights you pin with ...Bg4, give the bishop for the knight and build a French-like structure with no bad bishop. Against the Fantasy you play ...e6 and ...Bb4 against e4, or ...Qb6 against b2, and break with ...c5.

chapters.title: Early deviations: 2.c4 and 2.d3
chapters.intro: Against 2.c4 you strike with ...d5 at once and get a version of the Panov where your pieces are very active. Against the slow King's Indian Attack with 2.d3, take the centre with ...d5 and ...e5: White has given up the fight for the centre, so you get a reversed setup with an extra tempo.

courses.name: Caro-Kann Defence
courses.tagline: Rock-solid against 1.e4, with a light-squared bishop that never gets stuck.
courses.description: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5. Black supports d5 with the c-pawn, gets the c8 bishop out before ...e6, and reaches healthy structures with good endgames. The recurring ideas are simple: the light-squared bishop lives outside the pawn chain, ...c5 or ...e5 is the freeing break, and against an isolated d-pawn you blockade on d5 and trade pieces. This course covers the Advance (Short system, 4.c3, 4.Bd3, Tal's 4.h4, 4.Nc3 with g4, and the Bayonet 4.g4), the Classical with h4-h5 and all of White's knight tries, the Exchange and Panov-Botvinnik, the Two Knights, the Fantasy with its ...Qb6 pawn-grab trap, the Accelerated Panov with 2.c4, and the King's Indian Attack with 2.d3.

chapters.title: Advance Variation: 3.e5
chapters.intro: White locks the centre with e5 and builds a pawn chain: e5 is its head and d4 its base. Always attack a chain at its base. You hit d4 with ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Qb6, and bring the g8 knight to f5 by ...Ne7 or ...Nh6. Your light-squared bishop is shut in by your own pawns on e6 and d5, so you either trade it with ...Bd7 and ...Bb5, or play around it. If White takes on c5 instead, the base is gone and you strike the head with ...f6. If White plays a3 and b4 to grab space, you close the queenside with ...c4 and play on the dark squares.

chapters.title: Exchange Variation: 3.exd5
chapters.intro: After 3.exd5 exd5 the pawns are symmetrical and your light-squared bishop is free: the French's usual problem is gone. Play actively: develop with ...Bd6, ...Nc6 and ...Nge7, pin with ...Bg4, and think about castling long. If White plays c4 and ends up with an isolated pawn on d4, blockade it with a knight on d5 and attack it.

chapters.title: Tarrasch: 3.Nd2
chapters.intro: White's knight goes to d2 so it can't be pinned by ...Bb4, and the c-pawn stays free. You reply 3...c5, and after exd5 you recapture with the queen. White gets a lead in time; you get free development and an extra centre pawn. Most lines lead to the same structure: your e-pawn against White's nothing, with an easy position if you finish development. Watch out for sacrifices on f5 and e6 while your king is still in the centre.

If White plays 4.e5, the knight drops to d7 and you get the same pawn chain as the Advance, with your knight already on its way to b6 or c5. Hit the base with ...c5 and ...Nc6, then the head with ...f6. If White castles long, race on the queenside with ...a6 and ...b5, and use the b-pawn to swap off your bad bishop via ...Ba6.

chapters.intro: If White pins with 4.Bg5, unpin calmly with ...Be7. After 5.e5 Nfd7 and the bishop trade, you get the Steinitz chain again: hit d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6, then hit e5 with ...f6. With pawns on e5 and a bishop on d3, always check for the Greek gift sacrifice on h7 before you castle. The sharpest try is the Alekhine-Chatard Attack, 6.h4, where White offers the g5 bishop. Decline with ...h6, and if White blunders with Qg4, take the bishop and open the h-file.

chapters.title: King's Indian Attack: 2.d3
chapters.intro: Some White players avoid d4 altogether with d3, Nd2, Ngf3, g3, Bg2 and O-O. Grab the centre with ...d5, ...c5 and ...Nc6, castle short, and expand on the queenside with ...b5, ...a5 and ...a4. White attacks on the kingside after e5, so speed matters. Your light-squared bishop is not bad here, because your e-pawn is not blocked: it can go to b7 or a6.

chapters.title: Second-move sidelines and gambits
chapters.intro: White can avoid 2.d4 in many ways. Against 2.Nf3 and 2.Nc3 you play ...d5 and transpose to the main chapters. Against the Wing Gambit, take the pawn and keep it simple. Against 2.c4, take on d5 and play against an isolated pawn. Against 2.Qe2, switch to ...c5 and a King's Indian Attack structure.

courses.name: French Defence
courses.tagline: Counterpunch from a solid shell: ...e6, ...d5, then hit the chain with ...c5 and ...f6.
courses.description: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. You let White build a big centre and then attack it. When White pushes e5, the pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain: you hit its base with ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...Nf5, and later its head with ...f6. Your light-squared bishop is the French's problem piece, and this course shows how to free it or trade it. You get the Advance with the Milner-Barry Gambit, 6.a3, 6.Be2, 6.Be3, 6.Na3, 4.dxc5 and 4.Qg4; the Tarrasch with 3...c5 and the 13.Nf5 sacrifice; the Classical 3.Nc3 Nf6 with the Steinitz 4.e5, 4.Bg5 including the Alekhine-Chatard Attack, and the quiet tries; the Exchange; the King's Indian Attack; and the sidelines 2.Nf3, the Wing Gambit, 2.c4 and 2.Qe2, plus the traps that catch club players on both sides.

chapters.title: Early deviations: 2.Nc3 and 2.e5
chapters.intro: Some White players don't take on d5. Against 2.e5 you play a Caro-Kann-style Advance with ...Bf5. Against 2.Nc3 you can push ...d4 and grab space.

courses.name: Scandinavian Defence
courses.tagline: Hit e4 on move one and play your own game from the very start.
courses.description: 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5. You trade off White's e-pawn at once and develop around the queen: ...Qa5, ...Nf6, ...c6, ...Bf5 and ...e6. The structure is like a Caro-Kann, but White has to face it on your terms. This course covers 3.Nc3 with all of White's main setups, 3.Nf3, 3.d4 and the early deviations 2.Nc3 and 2.e5, plus the traps to avoid.
